title: Health at Home — Chronic Disease Management
lede: Health at Home was a chronic disease management service built for Telefonica, operating across O2 (UK), Movistar (Spain), and Vivo (Brazil). It was designed for patients managing long-term conditions

metrics.label: decrease in mortality rate | 63% decrease in hospital readmission rate

sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
Health at Home was a chronic disease management service built for Telefonica, operating across O2 (UK), Movistar (Spain), and Vivo (Brazil). It was designed for patients managing long-term conditions — primarily heart failure, COPD, and diabetes — who needed regular monitoring but could not or should not be in hospital for routine check-ups.

The service connected patients' home medical devices — scales, blood pressure monitors, heart rate monitors, pulse oximeters, and glucose meters — to a clinical platform that nurses and doctors could access remotely. Patients took their own measurements at home; clinicians reviewed the data, flagged anomalies, and contacted patients when readings required follow-up.

sections.title: The Role of Ethnographic Research
sections.body:
The design was grounded in deep ethnographic research with patients, family members, nurses, and doctors. Home visits with patients revealed something that surveys would not have surfaced: the nurse was the emotional core of the service. Patients did not talk about the technology or the measurements. They talked about their nurse.

As one family member of an 82-year-old heart failure patient put it: "Dad is all happy after talking to nurse Anna." The weekly call was the anchor of the service. Everything else — the measurements, the alerts, the data — was infrastructure that supported that human relationship.

sections.title: Designing Around the Nurse
sections.body:
This insight fundamentally shaped the service design. Rather than designing for maximum automation and minimal human contact, we designed a system that optimised the nurse's time so they could focus on the conversations that mattered.

The clinical dashboard was designed specifically around nursing workflows after co-creation sessions with nurses, cardiologists, and heads of department. Nurses handled the day-to-day monitoring, reviewing measurements and responding to alerts. Doctors were brought in only when a nurse flagged something requiring medical judgement. This division of responsibility reflected how the service actually operated, and the design supported it rather than fighting it.

sections.title: My Role
sections.body:
As User Experience Lead at Telefonica Digital/O2, I led the UX team across this project covering five locations and up to 17 people. I oversaw the ethnographic research programme, the co-creation workshops with clinical staff, and the design and delivery of both the patient-facing mobile interface and the clinical dashboard.

The patient journey map we produced from the ethnographic research became a reference tool used across product, clinical, and operational teams to align decisions about service design and implementation.

sections.title: Results
sections.body:
• 48% decrease in mortality rate among enrolled patients
  • 63% decrease in hospital readmission rate

These are outcomes that most healthcare products never achieve at scale. They are a direct result of designing the service around the clinical and human reality of chronic disease management, rather than around technological possibility alone.
